📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

Recent findings suggest that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World.

According to recent reports, the winning image reveals bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

According to recent reports, “I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”.

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more notable to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Photo: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World.

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World.

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World.

According to recent reports, I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

Sources indicate that you can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum.

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously.
  • But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear.
  • The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

Industry observers note that they left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families mentioned they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

It has been revealed that “Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office noted in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Sources indicate that rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

In a recent development, the next day, authorities confirmed they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

Sources indicate that the Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

Sources indicate that from 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before.
  • So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco.
  • Sources indicate that option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before. Further, they're experiencing FOMO or regret in not investing more in Anthropic earlier.

So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco. You get to pick one, and only one:.

Sources indicate that option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco. Free and clear. Move in tomorrow.

Option 2: $8.5 million of Anthropic stock at whatever it prices at, with a six-month lockup.

My first goal is to set the line like a bookie would, splitting readers as close to 50/50 as I can.

My second goal is to get you thinking about what the money is actually for. Follow the chain backwards. You take the job for the equity and hope there's huge upside. You want the windfall to buy a house. And you want the house because that’s where your family lives.

Option 1 hands you the end of that chain today. No lockup, no tax bill, no waiting. That is the whole debate.

Recent findings suggest that you probably noticed Option 2 is worth more on paper. That is not a thumb on the scale. It is the tax code.

A house and a share of stock are not the same currency. One is an after-tax asset that throws off shelter every single day. The other is a pre-tax asset that throws off nothing at all.

According to recent reports, to convert Anthropic stock into a $7.5 million house in California, you need $11.92 million of stock at long-term capital gains rates. That is 20% federal, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, plus 13.3% to California. A 37.1% haircut.

And that is the friendly version. If your shares are RSUs that vest at the IPO, they get taxed as ordinary income. Now you need $15.84 million of stock to buy the same house.

Quick note for early employees: qualified small business stock could wipe out a chunk of that federal bill. But Anthropic blew past the $50 million gross assets test years ago, so this only helps a very small number of people who got shares in 2021.

It has been revealed that so a $7.5 million house is worth roughly $11.9 million of Anthropic stock today. I set the line at $8.5 million because the stock also gets four years to grow, and the house does not grow nearly as fast.

I have a long-standing belief that equity in a company is a type of funny money. The value is based on growth and profit assumptions years into the future. A stock provides no utility. Its value can tank overnight, like we've seen with NVIDIA and many tech stocks recently. You can look at it on a screen, but that's about it.

Sources indicate that only when you sell it and buy something does it become real. And the moment you sell it, the government takes a third or more.

A house is different. A house pays you every single day in the form of shelter you do not have to rent. Your goal in getting rich from stock is to buy the dream house, not the other way around.

According to recent reports, owning that $7.5 million home outright costs $117,750 a year, and property taxes are almost the whole story at $87,750. Utilities, gardening, and services run $15,000. Maintenance on a freshly remodeled house is about $10,000. Insurance is $5,000. So “free and clear” still costs you $9,812 a month before you buy a single grocery.

Recent findings suggest that but renting the same house in San Francisco costs about $25,000 a month, a 4% gross yield. So owning it beats renting it by $182,250 a year, and that gap grows. Over the six-month lockup alone, that is $91,125 handed to a landlord while you wait for permission to sell.

Proposition 13. Your assessment is locked at your purchase price and can only rise 2% a year. If the house doubles, your tax bill does not. Meanwhile your stock's tax bill grows right alongside the gain.

In a recent development, the $500,000 exclusion. A married couple shields half a million of gain when they sell a primary residence. Anthropic stock gets zero exclusion.

You can borrow against it without triggering a taxable event. Try getting a line of credit against locked-up pre-IPO shares.

Recent findings suggest that and there is the part that does not show up in a spreadsheet. Your kids get bedrooms. You might get a rare enclosed front yard, or the sunset ocean view at 7pm. You cannot raise a family inside a brokerage account.

Now let me argue against myself, because the bull case is not stupid.

Anthropic's 2026 annualized revenue run rate is about $80 billion, up from roughly $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The organization also reported its first positive adjusted operating income, reversing a loss of about $5.6 billion in 2024.

It has been revealed that here is my pro forma, and I am deliberately staying inside the company's own guidance. I have the run rate at $90 billion by December 2026, $150 billion by December 2027, and $200 billion by December 2028. Growth decelerates from 67% to 33%, which is still extraordinary for a business of that size.

It has been revealed that if those numbers land, which I think they will because companies sandbag their first guidance, the multiple does the work for you. Whatever Anthropic prices at, that number gets cut roughly in half by the end of 2027 and in half again by the end of 2028. The company simply grows into the price.

Industry observers note that A house is not going to do that. A house is going to sit there and appreciate at optimistically 10% per annum, but probably closer to 5%, while asking you for a newly introduced roof.

Say you take the $8.5 million in Anthropic stock, ride out the lockup, and plan to buy your dream house with an enclosed front yard in four years.

The house is not waiting for you. At 5% appreciation, $7.5 million becomes $9.1 million. And while you wait, you are renting at $25,000 a month, which burns about $1.27 million over four years.

In a recent development, so the stock has to produce $10.4 million after tax just to get you back to even. Pre-tax, that means your $8.5 million stock has to become $16.5 million. The extra $6.1 million goes to the government.

Industry observers note that anthropic has to appreciate 1.9 times, from wherever it prices, within four years. Call it a double. That is an 18.1% compound annual return.

If it prices at $1.4 trillion, you need $2.7 trillion. If it prices at $1.5 trillion, you need $2.9 trillion. The dollar figure moves. The requirement does not. The house costs what it costs, rent costs what it costs, and California takes what it takes. None of that cares what Goldman and Morgan Stanley settle on tonight.

A 50% gain is not enough. Up 50% leaves you with $8 million after tax, more than a million short of the asking price alone, and $2.4 million short once you count the rent you burned getting there.

If growth keeps decelerating, from 33% in 2028 to 25% in 2029 to 20% in 2030, the run rate reaches roughly $300 billion by the time the four years are up.

So the real question is what multiple of that $300 billion the market has to pay for you to break even.

Mature software companies trade at 6 to 10 times sales. Run the math across the range and there is a clean dividing line at about $1.54 trillion.

Sources indicate that price below that, and break-even only requires an ordinary multiple. At $1.4 trillion you need the market to pay 9.1 times sales in 2030. At $1.5 trillion, 9.7 times. Both sit inside the normal band. The stock wins even if Anthropic gets re-rated down to a perfectly boring software company.

It has been revealed that price above $1.54 trillion, and break-even requires a premium multiple that still has to be there four years from now. That is a different bet entirely, because it depends on sentiment rather than execution.

For perspective, back in September, when Anthropic was floating a $2 trillion valuation, break-even required 13 times sales.

SpaceX went public in June at around $1.75 trillion. It surged past $2 trillion, then fell back. It has been a volatile stock out of the gate, and Anthropic may trade the same way.

That is the thing about a six-month lockup. You do not get to sell into the euphoria. You get to watch it, and then you get to find out what is left when everybody else's lockup expires on the same day as yours.

The other half of this trade is that San Francisco real estate is in a melt-up, driven by the exact wealth we are discussing.

Recent findings suggest that between January and late June 2026, 136 single-family homes closed at or above $5 million, more than double the 67 transactions in the same period a year earlier. In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million over asking. At the very top, even all-cash offers of $25 million and up have been outbid.

Industry observers note that this remodeled Victorian on Castro St. sold in September for $7,650,000 against a $5,495,000 list. That is 39% over asking, $2.15 million above what the sellers hoped for, for 3,416 square feet on a 2,622 square foot lot. Smaller than the house in our scenario. This is what the money actually buys here.

It has been revealed that A 4,500 square foot remodeled home on a large lot with views is a unicorn property. Homes with views usually don’t have large useable lots and vice versa. Maybe 5-8 trade in a given year. If you wait four years to buy it with your stock proceeds, you are not bidding against today's buyers. You are bidding against every other newly liquid Anthropic and OpenAI employee who made the same initiative you did.

Instead of the $7.5 million house being worth $9.1 million in four years, it could be worth well north of $10 million.

Recent findings suggest that that is the trap. Everybody's exit strategy is the same few houses.

Some of you are already typing that the answer is to take the stock and move somewhere a mansion costs $2 million. Two problems.

Sources indicate that the job that created the windfall is in San Francisco, so leaving means leaving the equity behind. And California taxes equity compensation based on where you worked while it vested, so moving after the fact does not get you out of the bill you are trying to avoid.

Further, would you really walk away from a job like that when there are so many more millions to make? Only if you’re a FIRE person who values time and freedom more than money.

Sources indicate that as for the mansion itself, I toured a bunch of them in Honolulu last summer and came away thinking buying a mansion in paradise might be backwards. Then again, having a mansion in a beautiful city like San Francisco is a pretty amazing combination.

According to recent reports, real wealth is not the number. Real wealth is the gap between what you own and what you can actually enjoy.

You can spend the next four years watching a ticker and eating at home to preserve optionality, and end up with $10.4 million and four years of your kids' childhoods spent in a sub-optional rental you did not love. Or you can spend those four years in the dream house, providing for your family and making memories, and end up with $9.1 million or more of home equity plus four years you actually lived.

According to recent reports, that noted, I believe Anthropic could reach $3 trillion in market cap by the end of 2027 and $5 trillion by the end of 2028. Against anything in tonight's IPO price range, that is a healthy amount of upside. If I am right, the stock wins this debate within about thirteen months and it is not even a contest.

I drew the fair line myself, and I am still leaning toward the house. Watching names like Google and Nvidia drop 30% to 40% in a few months is a reminder of how fickle stocks are. And not having to fight a bidding war over a unicorn property would save my wife and me a lot of heartbreak.

At 49 with two young kids, time is too precious to put my life on hold for money that won't be used. I might end up with far more money holding Anthropic stock. But by the time I sell and pay the capital gains, I doubt I can lock down the dream house at a reasonable price.

Because if I have $20 million in Anthropic stock in four years, so do thousands of other employees and investors. Bidding against one buyer is hard enough. Bidding against dozens for the same unicorn property is impossible to win. And what good is money you cannot convert into the thing you wanted it for?

So I take the bird in hand. I have watched enough people optimize their way through a decade and arrive at the finish line wealthy and vaguely disappointed. Money is a means to an end. And one of those ends is living in the nicest house you can comfortably afford.

Industry observers note that readers, Which would you take: the $7.5 million dream house, or $8.5 million of Anthropic stock with a six-month lockup? And why? Note: All your comments eventually go through. The spam filter is just working overdrive. Thanks for your patience.

Most people reading this will not be deciding between a $7.5 million house and an IPO windfall. But the same AI boom driving both is also driving something more boring: the physical buildout underneath it. Every model needs compute, compute needs data centers, and data centers need land, power, and permits. That is real estate, and it is the constraint nobody can code their way around.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.
  • The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday.
  • Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Sources indicate that turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek mentioned an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Industry observers note that cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

In a recent development, turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

In a recent development, according to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Industry observers note that jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet.

In a recent development, the Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

Industry observers note that the main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub.

Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Prepares

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.
  • ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months.
  • Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

It has been revealed that piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot problems in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Recent findings suggest that trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

Sources indicate that the members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Recent findings suggest that that led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Major List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

Sources indicate that the second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

According to recent reports, benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas remarked the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Sources indicate that jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the fresh performance category introduced this year in the massive list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It has been revealed that it is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

Industry observers note that as for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Sources indicate that buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term strategy is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
  • Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
  • It has been revealed that yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

It has been revealed that yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

Industry observers note that tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition proposal includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

It has been revealed that tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

It has been revealed that during a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

In a recent development, on a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that by late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Industry observers note that yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#45125. Latest Update: The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

Latest Update: The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.
  • I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares.
  • According to recent reports, but naively, I indicated a true order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.

I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares. That’s 4.6% of my indication, or about $5,000 out of $107,900. I entered my order the morning the books opened, hoping that would signal I was a serious buyer.

According to recent reports, but naively, I indicated a true order. I wanted up to $107,900 of stock to reach my goal of roughly $500,000 in Anthropic exposure through traditional VC, public VC, and direct ownership.

Sources indicate that the embarrassing part is that I should have known better. During my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, I worked on over 100 IPOs. I went on roadshows, introduced management to my institutional clients, and read demand back to the syndicate desk. Everybody padded their orders. A fund that wanted 500,000 shares would put in for 2 million because it knew the syndicate desk would cut it back.

According to recent reports, the problem with being honorable is that you lose when everybody else is inflating their order to get their true allocation. I thought being a Fidelity customer for over 25 years, with my kids’ 529 plans, custodial accounts, Roth IRAs, a SEP IRA, and Solo 401(k)s, would count for something. It clearly didn’t. To them, I’m just a number, like most people who work are.

Sources indicate that the allocation process reminded me that if you want to compete in this hyper-competitive world, you have to work the system to your advantage. If you don’t, you will likely lose to those who do.

According to recent reports, to protest my insultingly low allocation, I decided to take the day off. But that’s what I do every day anyway.

Here are some real-life examples where playing fair cost money, time, and happiness.

In a recent development, when my wife and I applied to preschools for our son, we decided not to ask our network to write letters of recommendation to the school heads. Despite having friends who were major donors and board members, I wanted to see if we could get in on our own merits as a high school tennis coach and his editor wife.

Sources indicate that we could not. Six preschools rejected us after happily taking our $75 to $100 application fees. We only got into our neighborhood preschool through serendipity. We kept running into one of their teachers on paternity leave in Golden Gate Park.

If we had leaned on our connections, we would have saved hundreds in application fees, dozens of hours, and a lot of stress.

It has been revealed that the families who got in weren’t less honorable. They were more effective. Our honor tax came to six rejection letters and several hundred dollars in application fees.

According to recent reports, I first thought about starting Financial Samurai in 2006, the year I graduated from Cal’s MBA program. But I didn’t because I felt I needed at least 10 years of finance experience before I had the credibility to write publicly.

Industry observers note that so I waited until the world was falling apart in 2009, 10 years after graduating from William & Mary. The three-year delay cost me revenue, likely earlier book deals, a bigger reputation, and probably pushed back my exit from finance by at least a year. I wrote more about this in Don’t Let Honor And Pride Keep You On Hard Mode Forever.

The internet has shown me time and again that you do NOT need expertise in what you’re talking about or selling. A not-rich 26-year-old can write a book on how to get rich. Someone whose marriage is falling apart and doesn't have kids can host a podcast for couples with kids. Someone with a $100,000 portfolio can become an investing guru on social media.

In a recent development, plenty of people overlook your experience or credentials. So you might as well put yourself out there and start.

It has been revealed that after 13 years of grade school and four years of college, you might have too much pride to accept money from your parents. Making it on your own feels like the honorable thing to do. It’s also good for your self-esteem.

Recent findings suggest that so you sleep on a friend’s couch and lose weight because you can barely afford groceries. Meanwhile, your college friends rent nice two-bedrooms in the city and go out every weekend because their parents are paying. Some even buy their first homes and have their girlfriends move in, courtesy of the Bank of Mom and Dad.

You, on the other hand, turn down an amazing job offer in Newly introduced York City because it’s way too expensive. Instead, you stay in Des Moines, Iowa, take a $60,000 job with benefits, and feel like you’ve made it.

Industry observers note that at your 10-year college reunion, you’ve finally saved $100,000 and are ready to settle down. But the girl you liked moved to NYC to be with your college buddy, who is now a director at a hedge fund making $1 million a year.

He’s worth $7 million and no longer needs his parents’ help. So he buys a $6 million, three-bedroom condo on the Upper West Side, marries your dream girl, and starts a family.

His parents’ help wasn’t a handout. It was a launch pad. Your pride was an anchor. More parents would rather help their adult children while still alive than after they are gone. Accept help with grace.

Recent findings suggest that in 2012, I wanted out of banking. The classic move would have been to give two weeks’ notice, thank everyone, and walk away. That’s what most people do, leaving their deferred compensation and any chance of severance on the table.

Instead, I negotiated. I offered to train my junior colleague to take over my business, which gave management a smooth transition. In exchange, I kept five years of deferred compensation and walked away with a six-figure severance check. That money gave me a multi-year runway to grow Financial Samurai and remain free.

According to recent reports, had I just quit, my honor tax would have been five years of deferred compensation plus a six-figure severance check. That’s an expensive way to feel good about yourself, when companies treat you as a number and quickly move on once you’re gone.

I break down the exact process in How To Engineer Your Layoff if you're looking to leave with a severance package as well.

You’d have to be naive to think a wealthy parent who virtue signals about how amazing public schools are, but sends their own kids to private school, would ever give up their kid’s college spot for yours.

The world is extremely cutthroat. Yes, you will have good friends and good people who try to help you. But in most competitive situations, you’re up against people who care about themselves and their families first.

Industry observers note that in my IPO example, my competitors were the thousands of other retail investors who wanted shares. If I had inflated my order by 10X, I might have gotten about $50,000 of stock instead of $5,000. With a 15% first-day pop, that’s a $7,500 gain instead of $750.

So whatever credentials or goodwill you have, don’t assume they mean much. At every competitive juncture, you must speak up and market yourself. People will forget who you are and what you’ve done for them if you don’t remind them.

Working the system doesn’t mean lying, cheating, or stepping on people. It means understanding how the game is actually scored so you stop paying an honor tax you don’t owe. Here’s how.

In a recent development, 1) Inventory your unfair advantages. Write down your network, capital, credentials, platform, free time, and family support. Most people underestimate what they have because they’ve never made the list.

In a recent development, 2) Learn how the game is really scored. IPO books get padded. Admissions offices respond to relationships and donations. Many jobs get filled through referrals before they’re ever posted. Find an insider and ask how decisions actually get made. The official rules are often only half the story.

Industry observers note that 3) Make the ask early. A referral, an introduction, or a note from a board member costs your friend five minutes. Getting rejected six times costs you far more. Most people are happy to help. They just need to be asked.

Sources indicate that 4) Negotiate everything with leverage. A competing job offer, a severance package, a retention offer from your cable manufacturer, a lower rate from your lender. If you don’t ask, the answer is always no.

In a recent development, 5) Accept help with gratitude, then pay it forward. Taking help from parents, mentors, or friends isn’t weakness. It’s compounding. The honorable part is what you do with the head start.

Sources indicate that 6) Remind people of your value. Send the update email. Check in with the fund manager. Tell your longtime broker you’d like a bigger allocation next time. Silence gets read as indifference.

Industry observers note that 7) Know your line and your risk. Padding an IPO order is common, but there’s a catch. If demand comes in weaker than expected, you could get filled on everything you asked for. Never inflate an order you can’t afford to pay for. Game the system, but don’t break the law or your word.

Be honorable with your family, your friends, and anyone who trusts you. Keep your word. Pay your debts.

But when you’re competing for a scarce resource against strangers, following an honor code nobody else follows isn’t noble. It’s expensive. And the cost compounds over decades in the form of lost money, lost time, and lost happiness.

If you’re a parent, it’s your responsibility to fight to give your children every chance to survive and thrive. Your kids won’t care that you were too proud to make a phone call. They’ll care whether they got the opportunity.

Sources indicate that as I wrap up this post, I have a confession. Maybe honor wasn’t the only reason I placed a true order.

Recent findings suggest that between my traditional venture funds and public venture funds, I already own a meaningful amount of Anthropic. So deep down, I probably felt my exposure was significant enough. If I had really needed those shares, I suspect I would have padded my order like everybody else.

In other words, maybe I just didn’t care that much if my order got cut by 95%. I’m at a stage in life where I should have enough. Missing out on a $7,500 first-day pop won’t change how I live, where my kids go to school, or what time I wake up tomorrow.

According to recent reports, which makes me wonder whether our actions show our real financial position better than our words do. The person who fights hardest for every share, every school spot, and every introduction is often the person who feels they don’t have enough yet. They say they are financially independent, yet stay for one more year at a job they hate. The person who shrugs may simply be full.

So before you judge yourself for being too honorable, or someone else for working the system, ask what each of you actually needs.

Sometimes the honor tax is a choice. Sometimes it’s just a sign you can afford to pay it.

In a recent development, have you ever lost out because you played by the rules while others didn’t? Did you pad your order in the Anthropic IPO, and how much did you get relative to your true demand? Where do you draw the line between leveraging your advantages and gaming the system unfairly?

It has been revealed that would you accept financial help from your parents to get ahead, or is making it on your own still worth the price? And if you have kids, how hard are you willing to work your network to give them a better shot?

Do you think your willingness to play hardball shrinks once you feel you have enough?

Sources indicate that most people don’t fall behind financially because they’re lazy. They fall behind because they play by rules nobody else follows. They accept the first offer, wait their turn, and hope someone notices.

Industry observers note that in Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller, I show you how to build wealth on purpose. It covers the right net worth targets for your age, how to multiply your income, and how to use every advantage you have to reach seven figures and beyond.

Sources indicate that building wealth also means getting the substantial decisions right. Buy This Not That, a WSJ bestseller, is my framework for life’s most expensive choices: how much house to buy, how to invest, how to negotiate, and when to take a risk. One good decision can easily make up for years of honor tax.

Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
  • It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
  • Sources indicate that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Sources indicate that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

Sources indicate that the expedition itself came from a merger of two prepares. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

Recent findings suggest that in total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

Industry observers note that the Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

Industry observers note that base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

Sources indicate that the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

In a recent development, the 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

In a recent development, on April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

It has been revealed that A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

Recent findings suggest that “What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he stated. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but noted that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Sources indicate that many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Sources indicate that camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

According to recent reports, mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

Recent findings suggest that A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He noted they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Sources indicate that roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts noted that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Industry observers note that haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He mentioned that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Industry observers note that axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

Sources indicate that the problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original initiative of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

It has been revealed that in their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

In a recent development, memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Industry observers note that the questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

#45123. Latest Update: Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3372 w)
📖 Baca
