#45086. Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2416 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.
  • Recent findings suggest that on solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done.
  • Cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.

Recent findings suggest that on solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done. And by job I usually just mean boiling water or, if I’m lucky during resupply, “cooking” tortellini. However, now as a backcountry guide I find myself cooking for other people much more often than just myself.

Cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal. Instead of ramen or Knorr sides, we are cooking things like egg sandwiches for breakfast, quesadillas with cilantro salsa for lunch, and backcountry fried teriyaki tofu with mixed veggies for dinner. So with all due respect to my original system, the BRS is not going to cut it out there when I’m trying to fry eggs or crisp up the edges of tofu.

These meals might sound elaborate, but they’re quite simple in the backcountry as long as you have the proper tools: I tested the Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L stove system this summer to see if it could get the job done.

Jetboil has really outdone itself with this one. Highlights include a do-it-all pot that’s large enough to feed the whole group, light enough to carry on the trail, and built with much of the same technology Jetboil customers already know and love, plus key improvements over past models.

Straining boiling water into a larger pot while cooking for a large group on the Lost Coast Trail. The TrailCook 2.0L would soon after be used to soft boil some eggs.

MSRP: $199 Weight: 1 lb 6.24 oz or 630 g Dimensions: 17.3 cm x 14.5 cm Boil time:130 sec/0.5 liter water Capacity: 2 liters.

According to recent reports, while I think the Trailcook is one of the best all-in-one cook systems available on the market today, there is a specific use case for this setup. This system is overkill for a solo thru-hiker, but it really shines when you are cooking for more than two people on a backcountry outing. If your idea of camp cooking goes beyond boiling water and into preparing actual meals for you and your friends in the woods, the TrailCook 2.0L is definitely worth a look.

I took the TrailCook 2.0L system out on several outings during my initial testing period, putting it to work in a variety of group settings. It fed me and my coworkers during a three-day training trip on the Tahoe Rim Trail, helped cook for 18 students over six days in the Gila Wilderness, and performed beautifully while preparing meals for 11 women on the Lost Coast Trail.

Across each of these trips, the TrailCook 2.0L consistently felt like it was the right tool for the job. It never felt bulky or difficult to pack, yet it always had enough capacity to handle the demands of group cooking. What started as a product to test has rapidly become an integral part of my kitchen setup on group trips, and I strategy to continue taking it into the backcountry long after this review is published.

Boiling water rapidly while students participate in a field lesson before dinner.

FluxRing: This heat-transfer technology is one reason Jetboil stoves are among the best at heating rapidly and efficiently.

It has been revealed that handling tabs and strainer: These user-friendly features let you drain the pot without burning your fingers on the hot lid. Hole for more exact pours on one side of the lid and strainer lines on the other.

Handling tabs and lid-lifter protected from heat.

Integrated 6,000 BTU/hr Burner: Powerful and effective. Just 130 seconds to boil half a liter of water.

Folding lockout silicone handles: Super handy for when the pot is full of heavy water or food. There is nothing worse than having to guess if your pot handle is going to hold.

Industry observers note that easy-ignite: The Trailcook lights just like a gas stove at home. The igniter felt intuitive and worked every time I used it. Keeping my fingers crossed it continues to do so.

Igniter with precision heat control features.

Sources indicate that precision heat control: This was a great feature for simmering or otherwise controlling the stove’s heat level! I haven’t seen this in the previous Jetboil versions I have owned, and I definitely suggest choosing a model with this feature included.

Compatible with accessories: While I didn’t test the stove with any accessories, the Summit Skillet will also fit with this system, as will the 1.5L cookpot, giving you multiple cooking surface options.

All-in-one packing: It’s so important to have gear that fits well into your pack. Despite this stove system’s large capacity, it’s so compact and easy to fit neatly into a backpack. The burner goes into a small bag, which can fit inside the pot along with a small (4 oz) fuel canister. The lid can then be put on and the handles folded to keep everything neatly packed together.

In a recent development, stove with igniter and fuel all neatly held inside pot with handles keeping everything together. Hand shown for scale.

Industry observers note that 2Lpot: The size of this pot makes it ideal for large-group cooking, such as on my guided backcountry trips. While a second or third pot might be needed depending on group size, this system always boils water the quickest and gets the cooking off to a quick and easy start.

Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of stoves on the market, but what makes a Jetboil a Jetboil is how rapidly it can take water from snowmelt to a rolling boil. It has an insanely fast boil time, and that has undoubtedly contributed to Jetboil’s popularity over the years. When you’re cold, hungry, and ready for dinner, those extra few minutes start to matter.

Industry observers note that the TrailCook 2.0L is designed for group cooking, and where it really stands out is in its combination of speed, efficiency, and packability. There are plenty of ways to cook for a group in the backcountry. For years, my setup was an MSR WhisperLite, a fuel bottle, and a large pot. That system works, but it also means carrying multiple pieces of gear, finding room for all of them in your pack, and waiting longer for water to boil.

The TrailCook 2.0L simplifies all of that. Everything nests neatly together, and thanks to Jetboil’s FluxRing technology, it boils water and cooks food much faster and more efficiently than the WhisperLite setups I’ve used in the past. It’s also not limited to just boiling water. The improved heat control makes it much easier to simmer, sauté, and cook actual meals instead of simply rehydrating food.

Soft-boiling eggs for the group. 6-minute boil followed by rapid cold dunk. Enjoy!

Industry observers note that what impressed me most was how much cooking capacity Jetboil packed into such a compact system. A two-liter pot capable of feeding a group could easily feel bulky or awkward to carry, but I never felt like the TrailCook took up an unreasonable amount of pack space. On trips where I was cooking for anywhere from a handful of coworkers to nearly twenty students, I was consistently glad to have it along.

According to recent reports, and while the TrailCook is certainly designed with the backcountry in mind, I think it deserves some credit for front-country camping too. If you’re cooking for two to four people, it offers a much more compact and portable alternative to hauling around a traditional Coleman stove and camp kitchen setup. You give up some cooking surface area, but you gain a lot in ease of use, packability, and speed.

I love knowing that when I get to camp after a long day of hiking or driving, my cook system is together in one place and takes just seconds to get going when it’s time to start dinner.

Recent findings suggest that there are so many features on the TrailCook 2.0L that I love. Below is my love note to each of them:.

It has been revealed that locking handles: Glorious. They lock out and feel sturdy and secure while cooking, and I never worried about them folding unexpectedly while moving a pot full of food around camp. A real blessing.

Industry observers note that lid: A design I found myself appreciating over and over again. Having both a pour hole and a built-in strainer makes draining pasta, pouring hot water, or straining veggies incredibly easy. It’s one of those simple features that feels like it was added after years of field testing and experience. It just makes sense.

Strainer side of lid, letting the water out while keeping the yum yum in.

No boil-over: If you’ve ever stood over a stove trying to prevent starchy pasta water from dumping all over your cook setup, you’ll understand why this is such a win. Even when I filled the pot well above the fill line, the contents didn’t bubble out like they did with some older Jetboil models.

Industry observers note that heat pads: The heat pads built into the lid sound minor, but they’re such a quality-of-life improvement. In the past, dumping water out of the lid usually meant grabbing a buff, a shirt sleeve, or whatever happened to be nearby to avoid burning my fingers on the hot metal. With the TrailCook 2.0L, this is a non-concern thanks to the little orange heat pads.

Speed: This thing is FAST. Jetboil has built its reputation on rapid boil times, and the TrailCook 2.0L is no exception. Whether I was melting snow, boiling water for a meal, or trying to get dinner on the table for a large group, I was consistently impressed by how swiftly it got the job done. It worked so well that I could boil multiple pots of water on the Jetboil before the first pot finished boiling on my Whisperlite when I had both stoves going at once.

Industry observers note that capacity: It was large enough to comfortably cook for groups — including one trip where I was feeding 20 people — without ever feeling excessively bulky in my pack. That’s a tough balance to strike, and this system nailed it.

Built-in igniter: Backpacking stoves have come with built-in igniters for years, including Jetboils, but they’re often unreliable and break easily. In contrast, this one worked reliably throughout my testing. When everyone is hungry and waiting for dinner, being able to fire up the stove with the turn of a switch is a beautiful thing. Goodbye, “which pocket is my lighter in again?”.

Heating rapidly is what Jetboil does best.

Recent findings suggest that pot support system: If I had one criticism of the TrailCook 2.0L, it would be the pot support system. I like the concept of the redesigned support arms and appreciate that the pot can be easily lifted on and off the stove. However, Jetboil markets the system as “self-centering,” and that wasn’t my experience.

According to recent reports, I often found it surprisingly difficult to tell whether the pot was properly seated on the support arms. The grooves on the bottom of the pot are supposed to align with the arms on the stove, but there isn’t much tactile or visual feedback to let you know when everything is lined up correctly. More than once, I found myself double-checking the alignment before feeling confident enough to start cooking.

That being mentioned, once the pot is properly seated, it feels stable and secure. The issue is getting it there. If one of the support arms misses its groove, the pot can sit unevenly, creating the potential for a spill if you’re not paying attention. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s one area where I think the user experience could be improved. I would love some external indication that the arms are in the grooves.

Recent findings suggest that weight: Again, this system shines in a specific use case. For solo hikers, the 2L capacity and 24 oz weight penalty don’t make sense. This isn’t a knock on the stove itself, which is meant for group trips.

The stabilizing arms shown along with bottom pot ring that sits on top.

Is this stove system worth my $199? My simple answer is yes. It has an overwhelming amount of useful, streamlined features and does the job well every single time. If I were in the market for a large-capacity Jetboil system, the TrailCook 2.0L would have my dollar.

Industry observers note that overall, the value-to-spend here is wonderful, but whether it’s worth it to you depends a lot on your use case. Do you need a large-capacity Jetboil system? Would the TrailCook 1.2L be enough capacity for your cooking needs? Do you cook for groups in the backcountry or are you a solo thru-hiker? Let these questions help guide your purchasing decision.

Shop the Jetboil Trailcook 2.0L Stove System.

So good even my dog loves it. DogBowl 2.0L?

MSR Windburner Group Stove System.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

It has been revealed that vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

According to recent reports, baia states the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

In a recent development, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin noted. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

In a recent development, bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

Sources indicate that this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” noted Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

Sources indicate that if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

In a recent development, red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

In a recent development, thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” noted Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

It has been revealed that once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the major cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

Recent findings suggest that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

It has been revealed that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

It has been revealed that conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

It has been revealed that in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin mentioned.

Sources indicate that “That is why it is vital to consider all options and potential problems before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

In a recent development, the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they remarked. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

In a recent development, they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing rapidly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles stated. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he remarked.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#45083. The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse.
  • I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water.
  • At 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse. After days of walking against the main flow of pilgrims, yesterday was the first time we had the trail mostly to ourselves—aside from the crowds packing onto the upriver boats.

I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water. Watching the sun light up the morning sky with a plate of boiled quail eggs and a couple of strong cups of espresso was a wonderfully peaceful start. Today was billed as one of the most scenic and spiritual sections of the entire Camino.

At 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water. The sun was just over the horizon, casting warm rays across the long footbridge as we crossed a small inlet bay to hike along the coast.

According to recent reports, after walking along the coast for a bit, the trail angled inland. Following a slight climb up to a small church, we made our first wrong turn of the day.

Once we realized we were off the official Camino, we decided to forge our own path using Google Maps rather than backtrack.

The route crossed a high bridge over a busy highway before diving into a peaceful forest. Climbing up, we looked back and were amazed to see how far away the coast already looked. We could see the bay, distant coastal cities, and mountains on the horizon—all after just an hour and a half of walking.

Sources indicate that as we exited the trees, we stumbled upon a massive vineyard stretching out across the hills. Unfortunately, the winery wasn’t open for another 20 minutes, so we kept moving. Walking through endless fields of grapes was incredible, and skipping the wine stop turned out to be a blessing given what the trail had in store for us later.

Walking against the grain of the Camino created endless confusion for everyone we passed:.

They became genuinely concerned for us, which we thought was endearing. Every time we ran into a local, we used a mix of butchered Spanish and sign language to explain we were hiking toward Porto. Other times, we just smiled, waved, and kept moving.

We were deep in the countryside, passing beautiful solid-stone homes with immaculate gardens and tiny backyard vineyards.

By mid-morning, we had already knocked out 9 miles in under three hours.

Industry observers note that we spotted the only café we’d seen all morning, grabbed a coffee and black tea, and relaxed on the porch overlooking the river. With such a fast pace early on, we assumed the rest of the day would be a breeze. We were very wrong.

The path ran right alongside the river for the next mile. The water was teeming with huge, two-foot-long fish—an invasive species, I assumed, since the river was practically overflowing with them. As the shade disappeared, the heat began to rise promptly.

Industry observers note that at the junction of two busy multilane highways, we tried crossing via an elevated pedestrian bridge. As we climbed, thick briers started crowding the walkway—a red flag I should have noticed sooner. Reaching the other side, I realized we were totally off-track. We backtracked over the highway and ended up at a massive roundabout packed with nonstop traffic. Fortunately, we spotted a pedestrian tunnel to get us safely across.

On the other side of the highway, we stopped at a small roadside restaurant. This was a crucial stop: there were no grocery stores, cafés, or towns along our next stretch of the route.

We ordered the local Pilgrim’s Menu:.

Before leaving, I refilled our water bottles from the bathroom sink, knowing we were heading into a dry, rural stretch.

The next 5.5 km section was advertised as a tranquil forest trail running along a bubbling river with numerous waterfalls, climbing gently up to the Mosteiro de Santa María da Armenteira.

Industry observers note that since we couldn’t get a room at the monastery, our strategy was to split off the Camino early and head to our accommodation in the tiny village of Silva. Armed with Google Maps, I figured it would be an easy shortcut.

Hot, tired, and out of water, we took a brief breather in a shaded cove when a cool breeze finally offered a moment of relief.

After climbing along the creek for 5 km, we left the Camino to forge our own path to Silva.

Recent findings suggest that what started as a narrow, paved road rapidly turned into a steep, unpaved logging trail climbing straight up through the forest. On Google Maps, it looked like a legitimate road; in reality, it was an overgrown, barely used dirt track.

I started to question: were we climbing all this way just to hit a dead end and be forced to hike all the way back down?

Knockerz was melting, I was completely exhausted, and we were both soaked in sweat and desperately thirsty. I hit that dazed, survival-mode state where you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, hoping the hill ends soon.

We kept pushing up the incline until, suddenly, the dirt track broke through the trees and met a paved road leading right to our door. Google Maps had come through.

Our lodging was a small, unmanned albergue with eight rooms and a shared kitchen.

Upon arrival our first stop was to hydrate. We went straight into the shared kitchen and drank glass after glass of cold water.

Next stop was to shower. We each took showers with our clothes on to rinse the caked-on sweat and dirt off both our bodies and gear at the same time.

Laying in the bed we were glad this day was done.

  • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

It has been revealed that “He was really lucky,” noted Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#45081. What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people.
  • In a recent development, but getting to the trail takes more than a dream.
  • Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

In a recent development, but getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

Recent findings suggest that 2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

Receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

As this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

Spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

It has been revealed that currently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

Sources indicate that donations play an important role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.

Help make the next journey possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

Recent findings suggest that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

It has been revealed that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed initiative.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#45079. Latest Update: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • Recent findings suggest that the journey has not gone according to plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

Recent findings suggest that the journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

In a recent development, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

It has been revealed that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

In a recent development, I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with newly introduced designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Sources indicate that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Recent findings suggest that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Sources indicate that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

Recent findings suggest that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

According to recent reports, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Sources indicate that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Industry observers note that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

According to recent reports, the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

According to recent reports, the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

Industry News: Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
  • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
  • As I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

As I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

The conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

“How do you find balance in your life?”.

This started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

According to recent reports, with three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were remarked as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

“No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

For the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

We laughed while we rested all together.

My Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

Recent findings suggest that the last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

Simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

Recent findings suggest that my Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

There was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

“I love these two so damn much.”.

And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last big day.

  • In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

It has been revealed that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

It has been revealed that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

Recent findings suggest that the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

Sources indicate that this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” stated Kondrashkin.

Industry observers note that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

In a recent development, on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.

It has been revealed that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m. on Saturday, November 14, according to a social media update. The hikers had lost their way amid heavy snow and treacherous trail conditions near the High Lonesome Trail, which sits near the Continental Divide Trail mile marker 1,340.

The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.

Industry observers note that an initial response crew traveled up Rollins Pass Road on ATVs before continuing on foot deeper into the backcountry. Upon locating the trio, rescuers found them cold and exhausted and immediately provided warming gear, food, and support.

Rather than waiting until sunrise, field leaders determined that keeping the hikers exposed at 11,600 feet in worsening conditions posed too great a danger. A second team was deployed to help walk the group out in the dark.

It has been revealed that rescuers hike into the night. Photo via GCSAR.

Sources indicate that rescuers and hikers reached the ATVs by 3:10 a.m. on Sunday, and all personnel cleared the field by 4:18 a.m.

Backcountry Conditions and Safety Reminders.

In their report, GCSAR notes that full winter conditions have already arrived at upper elevations, bringing deep snow, high winds, freezing temperatures, and rapidly shifting weather that can easily obscure trails above treeline.

Officials advise anyone venturing into the mountains to pack proper winter layers and carry the ten essentials.

It has been revealed that GCSAR is staffed entirely by unpaid volunteers. The organization never bills rescue subjects and funds its gear, training, and rescue operations through public donations.

Featured image: Grand County Search and Rescue.

Tech Report: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Recent findings suggest that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Recent findings suggest that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

According to recent reports, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Recent findings suggest that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Sources indicate that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Industry observers note that simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#45070. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It highlighted again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

According to recent reports, “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

Recent findings suggest that “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

In a recent development, during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s blueprint to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Recent findings suggest that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

According to recent reports, “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

According to recent reports, “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

In a recent development, “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

Recent findings suggest that “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang noted. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

According to recent reports, the climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

According to recent reports, climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

According to recent reports, strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Industry observers note that strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

Sources indicate that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.
